Part I: Text Mining of EFF and DA Manifestos

Text Mining Tasks

1.1

eff <- pdf_ocr_text("eff_manifesto_2024.pdf")%>%
   paste(collapse = " ")
eff_clean <- eff %>%
  str_replace_all("\n", " ") %>%                 
  str_replace_all("-\\s+", "") %>%                
  str_replace_all("[^[:alnum:][:space:]]", " ") %>%
  str_squish() %>% 
  tolower()

eff_df <- tibble(text = eff_clean)


DA_manifesto_2024 <- list.files(pattern = "DA_manifesto_2024.pdf") %>% 
  map(pdf_text) %>%
  unlist() %>%
  paste(collapse = " ") 

DA_clean <- DA_manifesto_2024 %>% 
   str_replace_all("\n", " ") %>%                 
  str_replace_all("-\\s+", "") %>%                
  str_replace_all("[^[:alnum:][:space:]]", " ") %>%
  str_squish() %>%
  tolower()

DA_df <- tibble(text = DA_clean)

tidy_eff <- eff_df %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(word, "[0-9]")) %>%
  count(word) %>% 
  arrange(desc(n));tidy_eff

eff_clean <- eff %>%

  map(pdf_text) %>%
  unlist() %>%
  paste(collapse = " ") 

DA_clean <- DA_manifesto_2024 %>% 
   str_replace_all("\n", " ") %>%                 
  str_replace_all("-\\s+", "") %>%                
  str_replace_all("[^[:alnum:][:space:]]", " ") %>%
  str_squish() %>%

DA_df <- tibble(text = DA_clean)

New_tidy_eff <- eff_df %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(word, "[0-9]")) %>%
  count(word, name = "EFF")

  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(word, "[0-9]")) %>%
  count(word, name = "DA")

   replace_na(list(EFF = 0, DA = 0)) %>% 
   mutate(Total_n = EFF + DA) %>% 
   arrange(desc(Total_n))
    
  head(eff_da_combined, 10)

1.5

cor.test(
  eff_da_combined$EFF,
  eff_da_combined$DA,
  method = "pearson"
)
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  eff_da_combined$EFF and eff_da_combined$DA
## t = -5.4655, df = 2974, p-value = 4.997e-08
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.13516817 -0.06402081
## sample estimates:
##         cor 
## -0.09972195

The hypothesis ‘The overall textual correlation between the EFF and DA manifestos will be low, indicating divergent ideological framing.’ is true. The two political parties’ manifestos are different in the language that they utilise. The correlation value of -0.1034108 is very close to zero and this indicates and confirms that the overall textual correlation is low. This also indicates that frequently used words in the manifestos of either political party are largely different from each other. This low correlation therefore indicates that there is very little shared word usage patterns in the manifestos of the two political parties; advocating for the hypothesis of there being divergent ideological framing.

1.6

shared_themes <- c("education", "employment", "infrastructure", "health", "housing", "jobs")

eff_da_sync <- eff_da_combined %>% 
  mutate(
    theme_type = if_else(word %in% shared_themes, "Shared_Development_Themes", "Distinct_Ideological_Themes")
  )

top_words <- eff_da_sync %>% 
  top_n(80, EFF + DA)

EFF_DA_Word_Frequencies <- ggplot(eff_da_sync, aes(x = EFF, y = DA)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = theme_type), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = top_words,
    aes(label = word),
    size = 3,
    max.overlaps = 60,
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Bivariate Regression: EFF & DA Word Frequencies",
    subtitle = "Highlighting shared development themes between the two manifestos",
    x = "EFF Word Frequency",
    y = "DA Word Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "blue", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, colour = "blue", hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

EFF_DA_Word_Frequencies

ggsave("EFF_and_DA_Bivariate.png", EFF_DA_Word_Frequencies, width = 9.5, height = 7, dpi = 300)

To begin, the “shared_themes” vector is a list of keywords that represent national development themes that both parties are likely to address regardless of ideology.

To account for the if_else() function, in the code: eff_da_sync <-eff_da_combined %>% mutate( theme_type = if_else(word %in% shared_themes, “Shared_Development_Themes”, “Distinct_Ideological_Themes”) )

The code says to go through every word in eff_da_combined. Then, if a word is one of the ‘Shared Development Themes’ then it should be labelled as “Shared_Development_Themes”. If not, then it should be labelled as “Distinct_Ideological_Themes” This aids in colour coding, interpretation, and bringing forth more meaning.

To account for this code:: top_words <- eff_da_sync %>% top_n(80, EFF + DA)

This is to find the top 80 words that appear in both the EFF and DA manifestos. This aids in plot clarity (focus and readability), labelling, and reduces word overcrowding.

These two codes are not redundant but rather complementary.

Hypothesis 2 states that ‘Topic modeling will reveal that the EFF manifesto clusters around themes of redistribution, nationalization, and state intervention, whereas the DA manifesto clusters around governance, market efficiency, and economic growth.’. and this is true.

Hypothesis 3 states that ‘If moderate or high correlation is observed, shared themes will primarily relate to national development challenges, such as education, employment, and infrastructure, rather than ideological alignment.’, and this is true to a moderate extent.

The regression plot shows a weak linear relationship between the word frequencies that of the EFF and the DA manifestos. There is a couple of shared themes, namely ‘education’ and ‘africa’; and, this is due to national development concerns and challenges rather than ideological alignment.

Part II: Sentiment Analysis of Data Science Course Reviews

2.1

The most appropriate dictionary to use for sentiment analysis is ‘bing’ which can be used on any text that expresses opinions, feelings, or evaluations.

Bing is then followed by AFINN and NRC. AFINN adds numeric scores to emotional intensity and goes beyond positive/negative labels and can be used to analyse sentiments of short to medium-length English texts, such as social media posts, reviews, news headlines, speeches, and/or letters. NRC. The NRC is used for English texts and identifies both sentiment (positive/negative) and specific emotions (anger, fear, joy, sadness, etc.). It’s therefore useful for any text where emotional nuance is highlighted; namely, social media, literature, and speeches.

Both AFINN and the NRC are secondary to bing, with regards to calculating the sentiment of reviews for the data science course from DSE University.

2.2 & 2.3

data_science_reviews_df <- read_csv("data_science_reviews.csv")

data(stop_words)

tokens_data_science_reviews <- data_science_reviews_df %>% 
  unnest_tokens(word, review) %>% 
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>% 
  filter(!str_detect(word, "[0-9]")) %>% 
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z]"))
  
sentiment_bing <- tokens_data_science_reviews %>%
  inner_join(get_sentiments("bing"), by = "word")%>%
  count(word, sentiment, sort = TRUE)

data_science_course_sentiments <- sentiment_bing %>%
  group_by(sentiment) %>%
  top_n(15, n) %>%      
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, n, sentiment)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(word, n, fill = sentiment)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~sentiment, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_reordered() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Data Science Course Sentiment Scores",
       x = NULL, y = "Count")+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))

data_science_course_sentiments

ggsave("Data_Science_Course_Scores.png", data_science_course_sentiments, width = 9.5, height = 7, dpi = 300)

2.4

The demand for the data science course at DSU University is very high, as there are five, positive high scoring terms like ‘helped’, rewarding’, ‘enjoy,’ ‘confident’,‘confidence’ used often by the students to describe their experiences of the data science course, and only one leading score term to speak on the negative element to the data science students’ experiences with the data science course;and, that term is ‘challenging’. The data science course being viewed as challenging is to be expected, as the nature of the course of high academic rigour. As such, the ‘negative review’ in and of itself is not entirely negative but rather a factual reflection of the nature of the high academic standard to be found, and is expected, in the data science course.

Overall sentiment shows and confirms that overall student sentiment is strongly positive, and supports the continuation of the data science course and vouches for the value that the data science course offers.
